Concatenate AnnData objects

Source: R/concat.R
concat.Rd

concat() combines AnnData objects along axis, following Python anndata 0.13.4 concat(). X and every layer present in the inputs are stacked along axis and aligned on the other axis by name, either on the names every object has (join = "inner") or on all names (join = "outer").

Usage

concat(
  adatas,
  axis = c("obs", "var"),
  join = c("inner", "outer"),
  merge = NULL,
  uns_merge = NULL,
  label = NULL,
  keys = NULL,
  index_unique = NULL,
  fill_value = NULL,
  pairwise = FALSE
)

Arguments

adatas

A list of AnnData objects. A named list uses its names as keys.

axis

Which axis to concatenate along, "obs" or "var".

join

How to align the other axis, "inner" (the default) or "outer".

merge

How the annotation of the other axis is selected, see the Merge strategies section.

uns_merge

How uns is selected, with the same strategies as merge.

label

A column of the concatenated axis annotation that gets the keys of the objects as a factor, or NULL for none.

keys

A name for each object (unique), by default "0", "1", ...

index_unique

A delimiter to make the concatenated names unique, as "{name}{index_unique}{key}", or NULL to keep the names.

fill_value

The value for entries an outer join introduces, see the Arrays section.

pairwise

Whether to combine the pairwise mapping of the concatenated axis, see the Aligned mappings section.

Value

An AnnData.

Arrays

With an inner join the names keep the order of the first object. With an outer join the names are sorted, unless every object has the same names. An outer join fills the entries it introduces with fill_value. The default is 0 when any of the arrays being combined is sparse and NA otherwise, so dense arrays become floating point. fill_value is an On-disk dtype in Python's terms: an R integer is int64, a double is float64 and a logical is bool.

Arrays are combined like numpy does. The result has the promoted On-disk dtype of the inputs, so int32 with float32 gives float64. A result is sparse (CSR, even for CSC inputs) when any input is sparse and dense otherwise. An array that only some objects have is kept on an outer join, with the other objects contributing fill_value, and dropped on an inner join. The same applies to X, and objects without X give a result without X.

Annotations

The annotation of the concatenated axis (obs for axis = "obs") has the columns every object has on an inner join and all of them on an outer join, with NA where an object lacks a column. Categorical columns take the union of the categories in natural order unless some are ordered, and bool columns become nullable boolean when missing values are introduced. The annotation of the other axis keeps the columns merge selects, from the annotations reindexed to the result's names. Columns of types that pandas would combine into an object column of mixed values (such as numbers with strings) raise anndata_unsupported_value_error. Keys are character, so numeric keys are converted to strings.

Merge strategies

merge and uns_merge are NULL (nothing is kept), "same" (values that are the same in every object), "unique" (values with one possible value), "first" (the first value) or "only" (values in only one object). uns_merge applies them recursively to lists. A function takes its place: it is called with the list of reindexed annotation data frames (or of uns lists) and returns a data frame or named list (or a list).

Aligned mappings

The mapping of the concatenated axis (obsm for axis = "obs") is concatenated for the keys every object has (inner join) or all keys (outer join). Arrays of different widths are cut to the narrowest on an inner join and padded to the widest with fill_value on an outer join, and data frames are combined on their columns. The mapping of the other axis (varm) is reindexed to the result's names and selected with merge, so it is empty by default. With pairwise = TRUE the pairwise mapping of the concatenated axis (obsp) is combined as a block diagonal CSR matrix, and otherwise it is empty. The pairwise mapping of the other axis (varp) follows merge.

Raw

When every object has raw its X, var and varm are concatenated with the same axis, join and other arguments, and the var columns and varm entries follow the rules for the other axis above. When only some objects have raw it is dropped with a warning of class anndata_missing_raw_warning.

Lazy inputs

When every object is read with read_lazy(), X, layers and the obsm arrays stay lazy (DelayedArray) and their realised values equal the in-memory result. When some objects are lazy and others are not, the lazy ones are read into memory, as Python does.

Deviations from Python

obs and var of lazy objects are always read into memory (Python keeps them lazy, loses their categorical columns and fails on an outer join with string columns), and a lazy result has DelayedArray's R types, not the promoted On-disk dtype. Annotation columns Python would turn into a mixed object column raise anndata_unsupported_value_error. See vignette("deviations") for the full list.

Examples

a <- AnnData(data.frame(x = c(1, 1), y = c(1, 1), row.names = c("a", "b")))
b <- AnnData(data.frame(y = c(2, 2), z = c(2, 2), row.names = c("c", "d")))
concat(list(a, b))$var_names
#> [1] "y"
concat(list(a, b), join = "outer")$X
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    1   NA
#> [2,]    1    1   NA
#> [3,]   NA    2    2
#> [4,]   NA    2    2
